sections.html:
Red Cherry Shrimp reach about 4 cm (1.6 inches). They prefer clean water with a pH of 6.5-8.0 and a temperature of roughly 14-30 °C (57-86 °F), and are most comfortable at a moderate room temperature of about 72 °F. They are omnivores and typically live 1-2 years under ideal conditions. Avoid copper-based medications with cherry shrimp.

There are various grades of Red Cherry Shrimp, from deep dark red to paler colors. The females are the most colorful and are particularly sensitive to the color of the substrate and background. In a tank with light-colored substrate they become pale or even transparent; in a tank with darker substrate they take on a fuller, redder coloration. Color intensity also depends on the type of food, water pH, temperature and water quality.

Red Cherry Shrimp adapt to a wide variety of conditions in the hobby aquarium. They can be kept in a desktop aquarium with as little as 2 gallons, but 8-12 gallons will allow for a more active colony, more breeding, and a livelier population.

Shrimp love plants and hiding spaces, so include leafy plants that allow them to sit on, groom, and feel safe. This is especially critical after molting, one of the most vulnerable times for the shrimp. They are also ravenous about eating the film of algae and micro-organisms that form on plant leaves, spending hours grooming their favorites. Shrimp also love to groom and hide in mosses, whether in a clump or tied onto a rock or wood.

Dwarf shrimp love planted tanks: they love the hiding space, the food plants engender, and what plants do for water chemistry.

Periodically, the shrimp will shed its exoskeleton, leaving a husk drifting around the plant. Do not remove this, because the shrimp will consume it and replenish needed minerals.

Feeding Red Cherry Shrimp is easy. Like many omnivores, they love variety. They will eat most any aquarium food but love shrimp pellets, algae wafers, blanched vegetables (zucchini, carrots, etc.), or more exotic foods on the market. Easy Shrimp and Snail Shells in the tank help keep the shrimp active and supply spirulina and other essential minerals, particularly calcium. Catappa leaves can also be a great source of food, as shrimp graze on the bacteria that break them down. Some enthusiasts report that adding a bit of natural bee pollen weekly improves breeding. Repashy foods contain 45% protein and are a great meal for shrimp, crab, crayfish and snails.

The key is moderation. It is easy to put too much food into the tank, which then becomes polluted quite easily. Shrimp are tiny and don't need much per day. Many keepers suggest feeding only every other day, or at least no food one day per week. Some also recommend removing uneaten food after 2-3 hours, depending on the number of shrimp, snails and conditions.

There are many nano fish that will coexist with adult shrimp but will also eat newly hatched babies. Even smaller danios, rasboras or tetras might eat babies. It is vital to have mosses and other hiding places, or even bamboo shrimp hotels that can easily be covered with moss. Smaller snails, nerites particularly, are a good addition since they help clean detritus and won't harm the shrimp. The best rule for fish is to keep only fish that get no larger than about ¾ inch as adults (chili rasboras, etc.) or none at all.

Red Cherry Shrimp are non-aggressive and active during both day and night. They can often be seen grazing on algae, hunting for detritus in the gravel, mating, and swimming from plant to plant during the day.

There are many varieties of dwarf shrimp. Not all can be placed in the same tank due to interbreeding.

Gender can be told by size and color: males are smaller and less colorful. Females often have a yellowish saddle on their back, which is actually eggs developing in the ovaries. Juveniles are almost impossible to sex until they are larger and show color.

Breeding Red Cherry Shrimp in the home aquarium is fairly simple if you pay attention to three steps: 1) inducing breeding, 2) ensuring health and comfort while carrying the eggs, and 3) raising the young.

Breeding is induced by keeping water conditions stable. Shrimp need a regular food source, with higher-protein foods (Repashy, Shrimp Cuisine, etc.) fed regularly in small amounts. It takes the shrimp about 3-5 months to begin breeding, with the female most receptive to the male just after molting. She then hides and releases pheromones into the water that call males to her.

Females tend to hide in the dark close to spawning and, if startled, may abandon their eggs. The more hiding places and the safer they feel, the more likely they will lay a full clutch. Once bred, the female carries the eggs underneath her, fanning and moving them so they stay clean and oxygenated, for about 30 days.

Baby shrimp are exact duplicates of the adults, but very tiny. Make sure there are no predators in the tank because most will easily consume a newborn shrimp. Live moss and shrimp caves help the babies hide and find food, especially microfauna that helps them grow.
